title: The Printing Revolution
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Before the fifteenth century, every book in Europe had to be copied by hand. A skilled monk might spend a year on a single Bible, so books were rare and extremely expensive, and only the Church, the nobility and a few wealthy scholars could afford them. Most people could not read, and ideas travelled slowly, usually by word of mouth. The invention of the printing press changed all this, and many historians regard it as the most important invention of the last thousand years, whatever their own special interests may be. Without cheap and exact copies of the same text, modern science, law and education would be very difficult to imagine.

The inventor was Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith from the German city of Mainz. Around 1450, he combined several existing ideas into a single system. The first was movable type: instead of carving a whole page on a block of wood, he cast each letter separately in metal, so that the letters could be arranged into words, printed, and then used again. The second was a press, adapted from the machines used to squeeze grapes. The third was an oil-based ink, which stuck to metal better than the water-based inks used by scribes.

Printing was not entirely new. The Chinese had been printing from carved wooden blocks since about the eighth century, and a Chinese craftsman named Bi Sheng invented movable type made of clay around 1040. In Korea, metal type was in use by the thirteenth century. However, the Chinese and Korean languages use thousands of different characters, which made movable type slow and impractical. Gutenberg's alphabet had only a few dozen letters, and for this reason his system worked much better for European languages.

Gutenberg's most famous work was a Bible, completed in about 1455, of which roughly 180 copies were printed. It took years to produce, and Gutenberg himself ran into financial difficulties, losing his workshop to a creditor. Nevertheless, the new technology spread quickly. By 1500, printing presses were operating in more than two hundred cities of Europe, and printers had produced about twenty million books, more than all the scribes of Europe had made in the previous thousand years.

The effects were enormous. As the cost of books fell, more people learned to read, and literacy slowly rose. Scientists could publish their results and compare them with those of others, so that knowledge accumulated more quickly. The Protestant Reformation, begun by Martin Luther in 1517, spread across Germany in a few years because his pamphlets were printed by the thousand. Standard spellings and grammar also developed, since a printer had to choose one spelling for each word and keep to it.

Not everyone welcomed the new technology. Some authorities feared that cheap books would spread dangerous ideas, and they tried to control printing by licensing the printers and by banning certain works. Some scribes feared for their jobs, and a few scholars argued that printed books were inferior, since they lacked the beauty of the hand-lettered page. Dr Ingrid Lang, a historian of books, points out that similar arguments are made about every new form of communication, including the internet.

Today, printing is taken for granted, yet its basic principle has not changed: a pattern is transferred from a master copy to many sheets of paper. Modern presses can print thousands of pages a minute, and digital printers allow a single copy of a book to be produced on demand. Even so, many people still enjoy the feel of a printed book, and sales of printed books have remained steady in many countries despite the growth of electronic reading, which suggests that the two forms can live together.
